newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukraine economy seen lifted by Russian visits.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine economy seen lifted by Russian visits.

text.p: Visits by the Russian leadership to Ukraine this week could help solve prickly economic relations between the Slav neighbours but only time will tell, Western economists and diplomats said on Friday.

"Establishing a more rational and less emotional framework is better for economic relations," one diplomat said of the two most powerful countries to rise from the ashes of the Soviet Union -- neighbours better known for their rancour than harmony.
Russian President Boris Yeltsin's arrival on Friday to sign a friendship treaty on Saturday was prepared by Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin on Wednesday.
He and Ukrainian Prime Minister Pavlo Lazarenko restructured Ukraine's vast debt to Russia, settled a lengthy row over the Black Sea Fleet and outlined economic cooperation plans to 2005.

"They're reclassifying the debt and that might be of some concern to international funding bodies. But it has been unserviced for so long, so at least they're doing something about it," the diplomat said.
But another Western diplomat threw cold water on the idea that the visits would provide a quick fix of economic harmony.
"I can't believe a visit like this will solve all of the problems," he said. "Russia wants Ukraine closer to its economic orbit and Ukraine wants to look to the West."
He said Ukraine was seeking alternative energy sources to reduce dependence and that implenting the Fleet deal would be difficult.
"On the economic side there will be ups and downs," he said. "I'll believe it when I see it when they say 'We'll have sweetness and light with Russia' about trade."
Almost six years into independence Ukraine's 50 million people are heavily dependent for energy supplies on Russia, their main trading partner with a population of 150 million.

Russia has often accused Ukraine of dumping cheap alcohol, tobacco and sugar into its markets -- as Russian businessmen have ignored much of the squabbling to invest heavily on Ukraine's Treasury bill market.
Analysts have also predicted increased participation from the Russian side once Ukraine's stock market grows and develops.

The first diplomat said Yeltsin, who has cancelled six visits in as many years to Ukraine amid acrimony over the Fleet, was showing a desire to concentrate on problems at home by cleaning up relations abroad -- and this was good for Ukraine.
"They're tying up loose ends so they can get under way with plans to kickstart their own economy," he said.
The Ukrainian side said Russia had agreed to restructure Ukraine's vast debt, put by Russia at $3.5 billion and amassed mostly between 1992 and 1994 for energy supplies.

"Most of Ukraine's debt is to Russia, and uncertainty about servicing it is causing considerable problems for budget planning and balance of payments," Ulrich Thiessen of the German Advisory Group on Economic Reforms of Ukraine said.
Ukraine had yet to work out a repayment mechanism, he said.
Ukraine's Deputy Foreign Minister Kostyantyn Hryshchenko said Ukraine must start paying $600 million next year, but did not provide further details.
Thiessen said it was a good move to set Russia's rent of Sevastopol to house its lion's share of the Black Sea Fleet, put at $97.3 million a year, against Ukraine's debt to Moscow.
